explanations.explanation: That's on the list, baker. The LORD says, “Cursing and lying, murder and stealing, and adultery are rampant…” (Hosea 4:2). When there's no truth in the land, lying doesn't have to fight for room. It walks right in and takes a seat.

Close to the neighborhood, but not what the LORD names. In Hosea 4:2 He lists “Cursing and lying, murder and stealing, and adultery…” and says one act of bloodshed follows another. Gossip and greed aren't on that list. Lying and stealing are, so those are the ones to remember.

I wish, baker! A feast sounds a lot nicer than this. But the LORD says what's rampant is “Cursing and lying, murder and stealing, and adultery…” with one act of bloodshed after another (Hosea 4:2). Feasting and singing aren't on that list.
Yes, the land mourns. The LORD says, “Therefore the land mourns…” (Hosea 4:3). It's a strong picture: the ground itself is in mourning over what's happening on top of it. That's how heavy this is.
A shaking land would be dramatic, but that's not the word here. The LORD says the land mourns. It's a quieter, sadder picture, like the whole place is grieving.
Overflowing is what my mixing bowl does when I get excited, baker. It isn't what the LORD says here. In Hosea 4:3 the word is that the land mourns, and the people who live on it will waste away.

That's what the LORD says in Hosea 4:3. All who dwell in the land will waste away with the beasts of the field and the birds of the air. Then He adds that even the fish of the sea disappear. Nobody is left out of that list.

Hosea 4:3 says it plainly. The LORD says all who dwell in the land will waste away with the beasts of the field and the birds of the air. It even adds that the fish of the sea disappear. So this one is true, baker.

Look at the second half again, baker. The LORD says, “You will stumble by day, and the prophet will stumble with you by night…” (Hosea 4:5). The prophet doesn't stay on his feet. He stumbles right alongside the people.

That's right. The text doesn't have the prophet staying on his feet. The LORD says the people will stumble by day, and “…the prophet will stumble with you by night…” (Hosea 4:5). The prophet stumbles too.

Yes, as His priests. The LORD says, “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you as My priests.” (Hosea 4:6). Right before that, He says, “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.” The rejection comes because they rejected knowledge.

Judges are a good guess, since this whole passage is a courtroom case. But the word in the verse is priests. The LORD says, “…I will also reject you as My priests.” (Hosea 4:6). Judges don't come up here.
Messengers do sound like they'd belong, baker. But Hosea 4:6 says the LORD will reject them “…as My priests.” That's the role named in the verse. Messengers aren't mentioned.

That's the one. The LORD says, “Since you have forgotten the law of your God, I will also forget your children.” (Hosea 4:6). The weight lands on the next generation. It's a sober line, so I'll just leave it right there.

Forgetting sins sounds like good news, baker. But that's not what the verse says. The LORD says, “Since you have forgotten the law of your God, I will also forget your children.” (Hosea 4:6). It's their children, not their sins.

Names are a decent guess, but the verse is more specific. The LORD says, “…I will also forget your children.” (Hosea 4:6). That's what comes after they forgot the law of their God. Names aren't mentioned.

Yes. The LORD says, “they exchanged their Glory for a thing of disgrace.” (Hosea 4:7). That's the worst swap I've heard of, baker, and I once got picked up out of a bin for 25 cents. Giving up the Glory for a thing of disgrace is a sad trade.
A crown of gold would at least look shiny, baker. But the LORD says they traded their Glory “…for a thing of disgrace.” (Hosea 4:7). No crown is mentioned.
A field of grain sounds almost useful, but it's not in this verse. The LORD says, “they exchanged their Glory for a thing of disgrace.” (Hosea 4:7). Disgrace is what they ended up holding.

Read the second half of the verse again, baker. The LORD says, “And it shall be like people, like priest. I will punish both of them for their ways and repay them for their deeds.” (Hosea 4:9). Both the people and the priest are named. It isn't only the priests.

Right, it's not only the priests. The LORD says, “And it shall be like people, like priest. I will punish both of them for their ways and repay them for their deeds.” (Hosea 4:9). Both the people and the priest are named, so neither one gets skipped.
That's the opposite of what the LORD says, baker. He says, “They will eat but not be satisfied…” (Hosea 4:10). They eat, and the satisfaction doesn't come.
That's it. The LORD says, “They will eat but not be satisfied…” (Hosea 4:10). They eat and they still aren't satisfied. I think that sounds like a heavy thing to live with.

Yes, understanding. The LORD says promiscuity, wine and new wine “…take away understanding.” (Hosea 4:11). That fits what He said earlier, that His people are destroyed for lack of knowledge (Hosea 4:6). It's a chain, baker: these things take away understanding, and without understanding a people comes to ruin (Hosea 4:14).
Homes are a fair guess, baker. But the verse names something else. The LORD says promiscuity, wine and new wine “…take away understanding.” (Hosea 4:11). It's their understanding that goes.

Courage sounds right, but the verse doesn't say it. The LORD says promiscuity, wine and new wine “…take away understanding.” (Hosea 4:11). That ties back to His people being destroyed for lack of knowledge (Hosea 4:6).
That's what the LORD says. “My people consult their wooden idols, and their divining rods inform them.” (Hosea 4:12). They go to wood for answers. I think that's a sad place to look.

That would be a different kind of visit. But the prophets of Judah don't show up in this verse at all. The LORD says, “My people consult their wooden idols…” (Hosea 4:12). That's where they go for answers.

The elders at the gate sound like a sensible place to ask. But this verse doesn't mention them. The LORD says, “My people consult their wooden idols, and their divining rods inform them.” (Hosea 4:12).

Yes, shade. The LORD says they sacrifice “…under oak, poplar, and terebinth, because their shade is pleasant.” (Hosea 4:13). Picking a spot because it's comfortable is something I understand, baker, since I wouldn't stand over a hot oven either. Here, though, it's where they chose to sacrifice.
Fruit makes sense for a tree, baker. But the verse says something else. They sacrifice under oak, poplar and terebinth “…because their shade is pleasant.” (Hosea 4:13). The shade is the draw.
A nice scent would be tempting, baker. I know a good oven smell can pull people into a kitchen. But the verse says it's because “…their shade is pleasant.” (Hosea 4:13).

That's the line. The LORD says, “So a people without understanding will come to ruin.” (Hosea 4:14). It connects to what He said earlier about His people being destroyed for lack of knowledge (Hosea 4:6). No understanding, no footing.
Scattered is a reasonable guess, baker, but it isn't the word here. The LORD says, “So a people without understanding will come to ruin.” (Hosea 4:14). Ruin is what He names.
Captivity is a reasonable guess, baker, but it isn't in this verse. Here the LORD says, “So a people without understanding will come to ruin.” (Hosea 4:14). That's the outcome He names.

Yes. The LORD says, “Though you prostitute yourself, O Israel, may Judah avoid such guilt!” (Hosea 4:15). Judah gets a hope, a wish that it stays clear of this guilt. Israel is the one being called out.
It's actually true, baker. The LORD says, “Though you prostitute yourself, O Israel, may Judah avoid such guilt!” (Hosea 4:15). That's a hope for Judah. It's not a charge against it.
Yes. The warning says, “Do not journey to Gilgal, do not go up to Beth-aven…” (Hosea 4:15). Those are the two places named. Joppa, Tarshish and the rest of the guesses aren't in it.
Those are good-sounding place names, baker, but they aren't in this warning. The LORD says, “Do not journey to Gilgal, do not go up to Beth-aven…” (Hosea 4:15). Those are the two on this list.

Those two sound familiar, baker, but they aren't in this verse. The warning names two different places: “Do not journey to Gilgal, do not go up to Beth-aven…” (Hosea 4:15). Those are the places it says not to go.

You got it. The LORD says, “For Israel is as obstinate as a stubborn heifer.” (Hosea 4:16). Then He asks, “Can the LORD now shepherd them like lambs in an open meadow?” A stubborn heifer doesn't follow easy, and that's the picture.

A dove is lovely, baker, and Minty, one of my cookie cutter kids, is shaped like one. But nobody here is compared to a dove. The LORD says, “For Israel is as obstinate as a stubborn heifer.” (Hosea 4:16).
A lion sounds fierce, baker, but that isn't the animal here. The LORD says, “For Israel is as obstinate as a stubborn heifer.” (Hosea 4:16). A heifer isn't scary. It just won't budge.
Not quite, baker. The word about Ephraim is, “Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone!” (Hosea 4:17). Nobody is told to go bring him home. The word is leave him alone.
That's right. The text says, “Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone!” (Hosea 4:17). It doesn't say to go bring him home. It's a hard line, and I'll leave it as it stands.

Yes, shame. The LORD says, “The whirlwind has wrapped them in its wings, and their sacrifices will bring them shame.” (Hosea 4:19). The whirlwind and the shame come together in this verse. Shame is the word the LORD uses for what their sacrifices bring.

Peace would be the happy ending, baker, but it isn't the word in this verse. The LORD says their sacrifices “…will bring them shame.” (Hosea 4:19). The whirlwind has wrapped them in its wings, and shame is what the verse names.
Favor would be nice, baker. But that's not what Hosea 4:19 says. The whirlwind has wrapped them in its wings, and “…their sacrifices will bring them shame.”
